## Python

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the share infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
sim.measles.plot()
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the share infectious
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # From I to R, after 8 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50))
sim$run()
sim$plot()
sim$measles$plot()
```

## Explicit

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
infection = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection')       # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the share infectious
recovery  = ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery') # From I to R, after an exponentially distributed time of 8 days on average
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(transitions=[infection, recovery], init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = ss.contacts(1), # Everyone mixes with everyone, with one contact per person per day
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = ss.days(0),
    stop      = ss.days(50),
    dt        = ss.days(1),     # Steps of a day
    unit      = 'day',          # The unit of bare numbers
    solver    = 'ode',          # Run as an ODE
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.plot()
sim_explicit.measles.plot()
```
:::

That is a complete model of a measles outbreak, written, run, and plotted. The rest of this tutorial explains it.

In Starsim, you write a model as an epidemiologist would describe it: the states people can be in, and the transitions between them and their rates. Starsim runs it as a compartmental model (equations for the number of people in each state) or as agents (one simulated person at a time). Starsim is in Python, and can also be used from R with [R-Starsim](https://r.starsim.org).

These tutorials follow one example: a simplified measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, for teaching rather than of any real outbreak. This tutorial asks: **how does an outbreak grow, and why does it stop?** [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd) covers the same model in depth, [Tutorial 3](t3_disease.qmd) gives the disease a more realistic course, and later tutorials add age groups, vaccination, several towns, and data.

You need only basic Python. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- write an SIR model and run it;
- plot its results and read what the run prints;
- check the model as Starsim has built it, with `describe()`;
- run the same model as agents, and look at individual people in it.

## Installing Starsim

Run `pip install starsim` in a terminal (or `%pip install starsim` in a notebook), then `import starsim as ss` in Python.

## An SIR model of measles

In an SIR model, each person is susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R), and moves along two transitions:

- **Infection**, from S to I, at a rate of β times the share of people infectious: β S I / N new infections a day, for a population of N.
- **Recovery**, from I to R, after about 8 days infectious.

For measles, β is about 1.9 per day: in a fully susceptible town, an infectious person infects about 1.9 people a day, or 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15 over 8 days. This is the basic reproduction number, R0, and 15 is typical of measles.

In Starsim, compartments are states, and each transition gives where people move from and to, and the rate (after `@`). Read `S >> I @ 1.9*I` as "from S to I, at a rate of 1.9 × I". This shorthand builds an [`ss.Transition`](../api/transitions.qmd), which you can also write out in full:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
```

## R

```r
states("S I R")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I)
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))
measles <- Disease(infection = infection, recovery = recovery, init_prev = 0.001)
```

## Explicit

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I)
recovery  = ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.days(8))
measles = ss.Disease(transitions=[infection, recovery], init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
```
:::

A state in a rate, like `I` in `1.9*I`, is the share of people in it. A duration, like `ss.days(8)`, is the average time in a state. A plain number takes the unit of the duration, so 1.9 is per day (`ss.perday(1.9)`). [`ss.Disease`](../api/diseases.qmd) puts the transitions into a disease, named `measles` after its variable; `init_prev=0.001` starts with 0.1% of people (100) infectious.

`equations()` gives the standard SIR equations:

```{python}
measles.equations()
```

Here `dur_I` is the infectious period (8 days), so `I / dur_I` is the rate of recovery.

## Running the model

The first cell gave the disease to a sim ([`ss.Sim`](../api/sim.qmd)), with the population size and how long to run (50 days), then ran and plotted it. The run printed what it ran (100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50), R0 (15.2, as worked out above), and what happened: the number infected, and the size and day of the peak.

Starsim ran the model as an ODE (deterministic equations), since nothing in it needs individual people. `sim.plot()` shows each state, and each transition as the number of people who made it each day. `sim.measles.plot()` shows the three states together: the classic picture of an SIR epidemic.

The curves answer our question. At first almost everyone is susceptible, so each infectious person infects about 15 others, and cases grow several-fold in a few days. But each infection uses up a susceptible person. Once most of the town has been infected, an infectious person infects fewer than one other before recovering, so cases fall, though β is unchanged. The outbreak stops because it runs out of susceptible people, not because the disease becomes less contagious.

With R0 = 15 and nobody immune, almost everyone is infected, and the peak comes within a week. Real measles is slower, since people are infected for about 10 days before becoming infectious; [Tutorial 3](t3_disease.qmd) adds this latent period.

## Checking the model

Starsim fills in what a model leaves out: here, how people mix (everyone with everyone equally, since no contacts were given), and how the time infectious varies (exponentially, as in the standard ODE). `describe()` shows the whole model as Starsim built it, marking each value it chose itself as guessed:

```{python}
sim.describe()
```

Read it for every new model, to check that it is the model you meant. Near the end, it says how the model is run (as compiled code or as agents) and what each rate is per step.

## The same model as agents

Starsim can also run the model as agents: simulated people who are infected and recover by chance. `n_agents=` sets how many; here 10,000 agents stand for 100,000 people, 10 each. [`ss.parallel()`](../api/run.qmd) runs several labeled sims and plots their results together, here the number infectious:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
msim = ss.parallel({'ODE': sim, 'Agents': agents})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

## R

```r
agents <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, n_agents = 10000, stop = days(50))
msim <- parallel(list(ODE = sim, Agents = agents))
msim$plot("measles.I")
```
:::

The epidemic is much the same, but the peak comes a few days later as agents, and the run prints a note saying why. Agents move one step at a time (by default, a day), and this outbreak grows several-fold in a day. With a shorter step, such as `dt=ss.days(0.25)`, agents follow the ODE closely; [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd) shows how.

Agents are needed when people differ in ways compartments can't hold, such as their own contacts in a network. Where everyone mixes with everyone, both give the same answer with a short enough step, and the model is written the same way. Most of these tutorials use the ODE, which is fast, and say what changes as agents: chance and differences between people ([T3](t3_disease.qmd#as-agents)), contacts between particular people ([T4](t4_mixing.qmd#contacts-per-person)), and interventions that reach people because of what has happened to them ([T5](t5_interventions.qmd#as-agents)).

## Looking at individual people

As agents, the sim keeps each person's state, and when they entered it. `sim.people.to_df()` gives a row per person (`measles.ti_I` is the step each was infected):

```{python}
agents = msim.sims['Agents']
df = agents.people.to_df()
df.loc[:, ['uid', 'age', 'female', 'measles.S', 'measles.I', 'measles.R', 'measles.ti_I']].head()
```

`agents.people.get_person(uid)` gives everything about one person, and a state gives the IDs (UIDs) of the people in it: `agents.diseases.measles.R.uids` are those who have recovered. [Array indexing](../user_guide/mechanics_indexing.qmd) shows other ways to pick out people, and [People and agents](../user_guide/populations_people.qmd) what each person has.

Starsim also has ready-made diseases, customized with parameters, such as the textbook `ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, and `ss.SEIR` (e.g. `ss.Sim(ss.SIR(dur_inf=ss.days(8), beta=ss.perday(1.9)), n_agents=5000)`). The Starsim library (`import starsim.library as ssl`) has fuller models of about twenty diseases, such as `ssl.Measles`, `ssl.Influenza`, and `ssl.TB`, used in the same way, e.g. `ss.Sim(ssl.Measles(), networks=ss.RandomNet(), n_agents=5000)`; see the [Diseases page of the model library](../user_guide/library_diseases.qmd).

## Exercises

1. Suppose people with measles were infectious for only 5 days, with the same β. What would R0 be? Change the model, run it, and check the R0 the run prints. How does the epidemic change?
2. Run the agent version of the model with 1,000 agents instead of 10,000 (each standing for 100 people). What changes in the plot, and why?
3. Using the output of `describe()`, find out how Starsim assumes that people mix, and how long people stay infectious (the distribution as well as the average).

## Further reading

- [Wikipedia: Compartmental models in epidemiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compartmental_models_in_epidemiology): the SIR model and its relatives, with their equations
- [EpiModel: Mathematical modeling of infectious disease dynamics](https://epimodel.github.io/EpiModel/articles/Intro.html): the same SIR model in R, as a compartmental model and as individuals
- [odin2: Getting started](https://mrc-ide.github.io/odin2/articles/odin2.html): an SIR model written as equations in R
- [Epiverse epidemics: Getting started](https://epiverse-trace.github.io/epidemics/articles/epidemics.html): ready-made compartmental epidemic models in R
